final.question: Signal from noise — you walk into operational chaos and leave behind something a non-analyst can run without you
final.object: The noise field: a drifting cloud of unlabeled data points, digits and chart-axis fragments, travelled through by one continuous camera, resolving into a different ordered structure at each stop and ending as a still grid

swap.reason: "Chaos in, structure out" is the default story of any data analyst and would sit unchanged on another analyst's site; only the Rent Map stop is particular to him.

backdrop.reason: The plan's own fallback replaces every 3D beat with a static end-state image and states "nothing is ever gated behind the 3D", so deleting it costs only decoration.

depth.reason: One camera travels from a disordered hero through progressively resolving stops to a fully settled grid at contact, so the order of parts is load-bearing.

clipart.reason: The resolved forms are an assembling dashboard panel, filter chips and a self-drawing bar chart — the stock emblem of the analyst job.

honesty.reason: The final plan prints the unmeasurable "35% improvement in efficiency", the wrong 40% reporting figure, and the hackathon as his own win.

thirty_seconds.reason: The hero carries only name and one line — "Nothing else — no subtitle, no button row" — so proof and any contact route require scrolling or hunting the dot-nav.

plain_reader.reason: "I make dashboards people actually use" is plain enough for an outsider and specific enough that a hiring analyst would respect it.

judgement.summary: A nine-stop scroll through one WebGL "noise field" that resolves into order at each section — three pinned case studies (Meridian, Helix, Lisbon Rent Map), then a lighter work grid, toolkit, credibility and contact — with a thorough, genuinely well-specified mobile, reduced-motion, no-WebGL and site-needs plan. Its weakness is the content layer: the concept is the generic analyst's chaos-to-order thesis dressed in dashboard clip-art, and having correctly flagged the source conflicts in reply one, the final plan hard-codes the wrong 40% reporting figure, prints the "35% efficiency" number the person cannot account for, presents a team hackathon win as his own, and plans to render the inflated CSV one-liners for FraudShield and AutoPilot as card copy.
